title: Generics
description: Generic classes and methods, type parameters, bounded types, and wildcards.

content.heading: Generic Classes, Methods, and Bounded Types
content.body:
Generics let a class or method be parameterized over a type, written in angle brackets: class Box<T> { private T value; ... } lets Box work with any type T while the compiler still enforces type consistency — Box<String> can only ever hold a String, catching type errors at compile time rather than a ClassCastException at runtime (the problem generics were introduced to solve, replacing the pre-Java-5 pattern of raw, untyped collections). A generic method declares its own type parameter before the return type: static <T> T firstOf(List<T> list) { return list.get(0); }.

A bounded type parameter restricts what T can be: <T extends Number> means T must be Number or a subclass of it (int wrapper Integer, Double, etc.), letting the generic code call Number's methods (like doubleValue()) on values of type T, which an unbounded <T> would not allow.

content.heading: Wildcards
content.body: Wildcards (?) are used when you need to work with a generic type without committing to a specific type parameter. List<?> means 'a list of some unknown type' — safe to read from generically (as Object) but not safe to add to (the compiler can't guarantee what type it actually is). <? extends T> (an upper-bounded wildcard) means 'some subtype of T', appropriate for a method that only reads from the collection (a 'producer'). <? super T> (a lower-bounded wildcard) means 'some supertype of T', appropriate for a method that only writes into the collection (a 'consumer'). This pattern is often summarized by the mnemonic PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

content.explanation: NumberBox<T extends Number> can call value.doubleValue() because the bound guarantees T is a Number. sumAll's ? extends Number wildcard lets it accept a List<Integer>, List<Double>, etc., not just List<Number>.

keyPoints: Generics (<T>) provide compile-time type safety, catching type errors before runtime
A bounded type parameter (<T extends X>) restricts T to X or its subtypes, enabling calls to X's methods
? extends T (producer, read-only) and ? super T (consumer, write-only) are the two wildcard forms
Generic type information exists only at compile time (type erasure) — it's not available at runtime
commonMistakes: Using a raw (non-parameterized) generic type, losing compile-time type checking entirely
Trying to add elements to a List<? extends T>, which the compiler correctly disallows
Confusing which wildcard direction (extends vs. super) applies to reading vs. writing
